results.title: Neuronal Overexpression of Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3β Accelerates Age-Related Glial, Vascular, and Inflammatory Remodeling of the Murine Dentate Gyrus.
results.summary: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN)-the lifelong generation of new neurons in the dentate gyrus (DG)-depends on the integrity of the subgranular zone (SGZ) neurogenic niche, which comprises astrocytes, microglia, oligodendroglial cells, and a dense vascular network. Although AHN declines during aging and is impaired in Alzheimer's disease (AD), the cell-type-specific alterations within the DG underlying this decline remain poorly characterized. Given the critical role of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) in AD pathogenesis and AHN regulation, we studied how the overexpression of this kinase in dentate granule cells (DGCs) remodels the cellular and vascular composition of the DG throughout life. Using a layer-resolved approach (SGZ vs. granule cell layer (GCL)) and mice of distinct ages (4-30 months), we quantified glial densities, cellular contacts, vascular architecture, and cytokine profiles in wild-type (WT) and GSK-3β-overexpressing (GSK-3β-OE) mice. In the former, aging was associated with a layer-specific reorganization, characterized by progressive astrocyte loss in the SGZ, midlife increases in GCL microglia, a reduction in oligodendroglial progenitors, and enhanced SGZ vascularization. GSK-3β overexpression accelerated age-related changes, triggering premature SGZ astrocyte depletion by 4 months, broader disruption featuring reduced SGZ microglial and mature oligodendrocyte densities accompanied by increased microglial morphological complexity, vascular restructuring, and a shift toward a pro-inflammatory environment. Therefore, neuronal GSK-3β overexpression promoted a non-cell-autonomous reorganization of the DG, consistent with premature remodeling of the neurogenic niche. These results provide mechanistic insights into AHN failure in AD and point to the modulation of GSK-3β activity as a strategy to preserve DG integrity.

results.title: The brain of the female Anopheles gambiae mosquito at spatial and single-cell resolution.
results.summary: Blood feeding in Anopheles mosquitoes is at the root of all malaria infections in humans and is supported by a range of physiological and behavioral adaptations. Since behavior is orchestrated at the level of the central nervous system, we surveyed the cellular diversity and spatial organization of the female Anopheles gambiae brain and compared it to other insect species. We then describe transcriptional changes associated with mosquito life history events with single brain and single-cell RNA sequencing. We did not identify expansion of specific cell populations, but a modulation of neurotransmission in the mated mosquitoes, and a metabolic and immune response associated with glia, Kenyon cells and immune cells after bloodmeal, and detected signatures of aging in the mosquito brain. We did not find an effect of Plasmodium falciparum infection. Our atlas will empower the study of non-model insect neurobiology, neural basis of vector behavior, and mechanisms underlying malaria transmission.

results.title: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange in Pediatric Patients: A Multi‐Institutional Landscape Analysis
results.summary:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
<jats:p>
                    Pediatric evidence for therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is largely small, single‐center cohorts; there is no prior large‐scale age‐stratified outcomes assessment. Using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we identified 3744 patients ≤ 17 years old undergoing an index TPE procedure, stratified into four age groups (≤ 1, 2–5, 6–12, and 13–17 years). ICD‐10‐CM diagnosis codes recorded 30 days prior to the index procedure were mapped to American Society for Apheresis Categories I–III indications; three high‐prevalence nonspecific codes were tracked separately. All‐cause mortality at 30 days, 90 days, and 1 year was assessed. All‐cause mortality decreased with increasing age at every time window: 30‐day mortality ranged from 16.8% (≤ 1 year) to 4.3% (13–17 years,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.0001). Infant mortality risk was concentrated disproportionately in the first 90 days postprocedure. Sex distribution shifted from a slight male predominance in infancy and early childhood (55%–56% male) to a female predominance in adolescence (55% female,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.0001). Leading specific indications were autoimmune encephalitis (10%), sepsis with multiorgan failure (9%), renal transplant rejection (6%), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (5%), Guillain–Barré syndrome (5%), and myasthenia gravis (4%); nonspecific diagnosis codes were each individually more prevalent than any single ASFA‐mapped indication. This is the first large‐scale, age‐stratified, multi‐institutional characterization of pediatric TPE. We identified an inverse relationship between age and all‐cause mortality, a sex‐distribution shift in adolescence, and an indication landscape dominated by nonspecific diagnosis codes. These findings offer age‐stratified benchmarks for clinical counseling and hypothesis generation.
                  </jats:p>

results.title: Chronic Lower Limb Edema in People with Multiple Sclerosis: Prevalence, Cause and Impact
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Chronic lower limb edema (CLLE) is a feature of advanced multiple sclerosis (MS) but its prevalence and causative factors are not clearly established. The aims of the study were to determine the prevalence and possible causative factors of CLLE in people with MS, and to examine the impact of CLLE on participants’ quality of life.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods and Results:</jats:title>
<jats:p>
                      The prevalence of CLLE was determined by questionnaire (i.e., self-reported) and by clinical examination. Possible causative factors were recorded including level of disability using Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) and the impact on participants’ quality of life was assessed using LYMQOL. The self-reported prevalence of CLLE was 42.4% (101/238). The prevalence determined by clinical assessment was 61.9% (99/160). Possible causative factors were shown to include age, reduced mobility, and vasomotor autonomic dysfunction. In the multivariate analysis, only EDSS was statistically significant (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.002) with an incidence rate ratio (sd) of 2.1 (0.52). In those with CLLE, scores in the function, appearance, and symptom domains of LYMQOL demonstrated a poorer quality of life. There was a higher incidence of cellulitis in those with CLLE (14% compared with 2%).
                    </jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
<jats:p>CLLE is a common problem is people with MS but may not always be recognized by patients. It can impact a person’s quality of life and poses a risk of cellulitis. Improved recognition and treatment of CLLE should improve the quality of life of people with MS.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Soluble TIM-3 and galectin-9 in cerebrospinal fluid are associated with disability at 6 months in aquaporin-4 IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background</jats:title>
<jats:p>Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders (NMOSD) are severe autoimmune diseases of the central nervous system characterized by autoantibodies against aquaporin 4 (AQP4-IgG). Despite the availability of several molecular targeted therapies, biomarkers capable of predicting subsequent disability early during the acute relapse phase remain insufficient. Given that abnormalities in immune checkpoint molecules are known to be involved in autoimmunity, this study investigated whether immune checkpoint-related molecules in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of acute-phase AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD patients correlate with disability at 6 months.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>Thirty-four patients with AQP4 IgG-positive NMOSD, 10 patients with myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD)at disease flare, and 11 patients with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) as control non-inflammatory neurological disease were enrolled. Bead-based multiplex assays were used to quantify levels of immune checkpoint molecules and related factors (PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4, TIM-3, galectin-9, LAG-3, 4-1BB, B7.2, IL-2Rα, TGF-β1, FasL) in CSF. These molecules were measured in the soluble fraction. Disease severity at 6 months was classified as mild (EDSS < 6) or severe (EDSS ≥ 6). ROC analysis was performed to evaluate prognostic performance.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>Twenty-six cases of NMOSD showed mild disability, and 8 cases showed severe disability. All cases of MOGAD showed mild disability. Compared to the mild group, the severe group had higher age, a higher male ratio, and higher cerebrospinal fluid protein levels (p=0.004, p=0.017, p<0.001, respectively). Cerebrospinal fluid levels of TIM-3, galectin-9, and IL-2Rα were significantly higher in the severe group (p=0.011, p=0.008, p=0.006, respectively), with area under the ROC curve values of 0.89, 0.88, and 0.80, respectively.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
<jats:p>In AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD patients, elevated levels of TIM-3, galectin-9, and IL-2Rα in CSF during the acute attack phase correlate with worsening disability severity at 6 months. These findings suggest their potential as early prognostic biomarkers, which requires validation in a large cohort.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Identification of Succinylation-Related Transcriptional Signatures in Alzheimer’s Disease: Integrated Bioinformatics Analysis and Clinical Validation
results.summary:
Mol Neurobiol. 2026 Oct 19;63(1):978. doi: 10.1007/s12035-026-06275-z.

ABSTRACT

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, proteostasis imbalance, and immune-inflammatory alterations. Protein succinylation is closely linked to mitochondrial metabolic status, but peripheral blood transcriptomic signatures related to succinylation in AD remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to identify peripheral blood transcriptional candidate biomarkers associated with a predefined succinylation-related gene set in AD. The GSE63061 dataset was used as the discovery cohort, and GSE63060 served as an external validation cohort. Differential expression analysis, ssGSEA-derived succinylation scoring, and WGCNA were integrated with a predefined succinylation-related gene set. Candidate biomarkers were then refined through four feature selection approaches: LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE, and Boruta, and their discriminatory performance was evaluated by ROC analysis, nomogram construction, calibration analysis, decision curve analysis, and SHAP analysis. Functional enrichment, GSVA/GSEA, GeneMANIA, immune-cell signature analysis, and single-cell analyses were used to explore biological relevance and cellular distribution. qRT-PCR was performed using peripheral blood-derived PBMC samples for experimental validation. Five genes, NDUFA1, NDUFS5, RPS27A, AIF1, and PRDX1, were identified as candidate biomarkers associated with a succinylation-related transcriptional signature in AD. These genes were mainly involved in mitochondrial complex I activity, oxidative phosphorylation, ribosomal function, protein homeostasis, redox balance, and immune inflammation. Immune-cell signatures and single-cell analyses further suggested that the signature was associated with T cells, B cells, NK cells, and monocytes/macrophages. qRT-PCR confirmed significant downregulation of all five genes in AD PBMC samples (P < 0.05). These findings suggest that peripheral blood transcriptional signatures associated with succinylation-related genes may provide candidate biomarkers and hypothesis-generating clues for AD.

results.title: Exercise promotes lipophagy and mitigates cognitive impairment in Alzheimer’s disease through downregulating microglial TMEM9
results.summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background</jats:title>
<jats:p>Autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction contributes to lipid droplet (LD) accumulation, which drives pathological progression in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Exercise is reported to restore autophagy-lysosomal function and attenuate cognitive impairment in AD, but its regulation of LD deposition remains unknown.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>5×FAD transgenic mice underwent a three-month exercise intervention. Cognitive and emotional behaviors were assessed using the Morris water maze, novel object recognition, and open field test. LD deposition was evaluated by oil red O and BODIPY staining. Proteomic sequencing was performed to identify proteins affected by exercise. Pathological changes were examined by immunofluorescence, western blotting, and transmission electron microscopy. Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV was used to overexpress or knock down microglial TMEM9 to investigate the mechanisms by which physical exercise affects behavior and pathology in AD. In vitro, BV2 cells were cultured and incubated with oligomeric amyloid-β (oAβ), with or without oleic acid to induce LD formation. Chloroquine and rapamycin, which regulate autophagy-lysosomal function, were used to examine the effects of LDs on mitochondrial integrity under glucose deprivation conditions. Lentiviral or plasmid transfection was used to explore the key role of TMEM9 in regulating lipophagy, and the interaction between TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 was detected by co-immunoprecipitation. Clinically, plasma TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 levels  in AD patients were measured by ELISA, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate diagnostic performance.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>
                      Exercise mitigated cerebral LD deposition through enhanced lipophagy, preserving mitochondrial integrity and attenuating cognitive decline. Mechanistically, exercise suppressed microglial TMEM9 expression, restoring LD degradation.
                      <jats:italic>Tmem9</jats:italic>
                      downregulation facilitated LKB1 lysosomal translocation, activating AMPK signaling. In vitro, oleic acid-induced LDs preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and increased ATP production in BV2 microglia under glucose deprivation and oAβ exposure.
                      <jats:italic>Tmem9</jats:italic>
                      overexpression exacerbated lipophagy impairment and mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas
                      <jats:italic>Tmem9</jats:italic>
                      knockdown enhanced lipophagy and cytoprotection. Aβ clearance was negatively regulated by TMEM9. Clinically, AD patients exhibited characteristic Aβ deposition and glucose hypometabolism, with plasma TMEM9 levels strongly correlating with p-tau217 progression. Plasma TMEM9 and the TMEM9/ATP6AP1 ratio emerged as potential AD diagnostic biomarkers (AUC=0.791 and 0.853, respectively).
                    </jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
<jats:p>These findings establish exercise-induced TMEM9 inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy targeting lipidostasis to combat AD progression.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: De novo formation of familial Alzheimer’s disease-relevant Aβ strains occurs exclusively in the human brain
results.summary:
Acta Neuropathol Commun. 2026 Jul 24;14(1):218. doi: 10.1186/s40478-026-02390-z.

ABSTRACT

In familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD), mutations in the amyloid precursor protein gene (APP) accelerate the aggregation of Aβ peptide, leading to deposition of amyloid plaques within the brain. Conformational variants of Aβ aggregates ("Aβ strains") possess distinct pathological properties and may contribute to disease heterogeneity. While the Swedish APP mutation produces wild-type (WT) Aβ, the Arctic APP mutation generates E22G-mutant Aβ. To clarify whether different FAD mutations are sufficient to specify the formation of distinct Aβ strains, we performed Aβ seeding studies in AppNL-F knock-in mice. Aβ aggregates purified from Swedish and Arctic FAD human brains induced distinct neuropathological signatures, characterized by differences in the morphology and localization of the seeded Aβ deposits, which were preserved upon serial passage. Neither synthetic E22G-mutant Aβ aggregates nor Aβ aggregates isolated from the brains of transgenic mice producing E22G-mutant Aβ recapitulated the phenotype induced by Arctic FAD brain-derived Aβ aggregates upon injection into AppNL-F mice. Similarly, neither synthetic WT Aβ aggregates nor Aβ aggregates from Swedish APP-mutant transgenic mice reproduced the seeding behavior of Swedish FAD brain-derived Aβ aggregates. This suggests that it is the structure of Aβ aggregates rather than the Aβ sequence that dictates seeding activity. We conclude that de novo formation of FAD-relevant Aβ strains occurs exclusively in the human brain, implying the existence of human brain-specific cofactors that modulate Aβ aggregate structure and seeding activity.

results.title: Real‐World Patient Eligibility for Alzheimer's Disease Anti‐Amyloid Therapy in Seven Swedish Memory Clinics
results.summary:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Background</jats:title>
<jats:p>Anti‐amyloid therapies lecanemab and donanemab are the first potentially disease‐modifying treatments for Alzheimer's disease (AD) approved in Europe. We estimated real‐world eligibility for these treatments in a large multicenter memory clinic patient cohort in Sweden (MemClin).</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
<jats:p>MemClin included patients with a first diagnostic visit between 2016 and 2022 at seven specialist memory clinics in Stockholm, Sweden. To estimate eligibility for anti‐amyloid therapy, we applied key inclusion/exclusion criteria from the lecanemab and donanemab appropriate use recommendations. Eligible patients were required to have (1) a clinical diagnosis of AD‐type dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI), (2) confirmed Aβ pathology (abnormal CSF Aβ42) and (3) no apparent medical exclusion criteria. Eligibility was calculated for different scenarios to provide both upper‐bound estimates (main analysis) and more conservative, implementation‐ready estimates of near‐term treatable patients (sensitivity analysis).</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results</jats:title>
<jats:p>Cohort consisted of 2126 patients (mean age 77.1 ± 6.6 years; 61.8% MCI, 24.2% dementia, 13.7% subjective cognitive impairment). In the main analysis, 11.5% of the whole cohort was estimated to be eligible for either treatment (lecanemab 10.6%, donanemab 11.5%). Most eligible patients had early‐stage disease (61.9% MCI vs. 38.1% dementia) and an A + T– biomarker profile, that is, normal biomarker of tau (57.9%). Eligibility was markedly lower in sensitivity analyses (e.g., 2.7% when all patients without MRI were assumed ineligible).</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
<jats:p>Even upper‐bound estimates indicate that a minority of real‐world memory clinic patients may currently qualify for anti‐amyloid therapy. These findings provide timely evidence to inform the ongoing debate on the implementation of anti‐amyloid therapy in public healthcare.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: MicroRNAs and polymorphisms influencing MICA immune modulation
results.summary: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that play a central role in post-transcriptional gene regulation. They act mainly by interacting with sequences located in the 3′ untranslated regions (3′UTRs) of messenger RNAs (mRNAs), thereby influencing mRNA stability and translation. Through these mechanisms, miRNAs contribute to the fine-tuning of multiple biological pathways, including immune activation, inflammatory signaling, and cellular stress responses. Among the genes involved in immune surveillance, the major histocompatibility complex class I polypeptide-related sequence A (MICA) has emerged as an important target for post-transcriptional regulation due to its role as a ligand for the activating receptor NKG2D (natural killer cell group 2-D), which is expressed in natural killer (NK) cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. MICA is highly polymorphic, and several allelic variants differ in sequence composition, structural organization, and expression patterns, potentially influencing miRNA–mRNA interactions. Growing evidence suggests that miRNA-mediated regulation of MICA contributes to immune modulation in cancer, viral infections, and autoimmune disorders, particularly through mechanisms associated with immune evasion and altered NKG2D signaling. In addition, genetic polymorphisms and structural variations within regulatory regions, especially within the 3′UTR, can alter miRNA binding affinity by creating, disrupting, or modifying target sites. This mini review discusses the current understanding of miRNA-mediated regulation of MICA, emphasizing the impact of allelic diversity and regulatory polymorphisms on post-transcriptional control. Furthermore, it highlights current knowledge gaps and future perspectives regarding allele-specific regulation.
